newsitem.title: UK: New N. Irish police complaints system proposed.
newsitem.headline: New N. Irish police complaints system proposed.

text.p: An official report proposed sweeping changes on Thursday to boost flagging public confidence in the way complaints against police are probed in troubled Northern Ireland.
It said investigations of serious complaints, including alleged crimes, should be handed over to a new powerful independent ombudsman and taken out of the hands of the police.

"The need for these changes is because there isn't public confidence in the system at the moment," said Maurice Hayes, a former senior Northern Ireland civil servant called in by Britain to carry out the report.

Hayes said that a judge, backed by team of investigators, should be appointed to a new role of Police Ombudsman "responsible to Parliament with a duty to investigate complaints and to report his/her findings".

The region's Irish Catholic minority, many of whom distrust the pro-British police force, say that under the current system the 92 per cent Protestant Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police "investigate themselves".
In his report, Hayes said: "The overwhelming message I got from nearly all sides and from all political parties was the need for the investigation to be independent and to be seen to be independent.

"While there were systemic failings in the present arrangements, they lacked credibility because of lack of independence, because it was up to the Chief Constable (police chief) who decided what was a complaint...and because the complaints were investigated by police officers."
A separate civilian "independent commission for police complaints", with limited powers, supervises the RUC investigation of 10 per cent of the more serious cases, Hayes told Reuters in an interview.

Hayes said his proposals were "partly" aimed at easing Catholic distrust, but added: "They are not designed for that. They are designed to produce a system of complaints in which the public generally would have confidence and in which the police would have some sort of confidence and reliability, too."

Sectarian clashes last year and a rising threat by rival guerrillas fighting over the future of British rule have pitched the RUC into a front-line security role, hindering plans for a full-scale return to "normal" policing, officers say.

It was the second major RUC reform report in two days. On Tuesday a British police monitoring body said the RUC should curb its use of plastic bullets, which pro-Irish nationalists and human rights group blame for the deaths of at least 16 people during riots and other incidents.
RUC Chief Constable, Ronnie Flanagan says plastic bullets are vital to reduce the risk to life and property during unrest.
